web_evidence.title: Point of View in The Da Vinci Code
web_evidence.note: This scholarly stylistic study samples the beginning, middle, ending, and epilogue and classifies the novel as Category B Reflector, explicitly defined as third-person narrative; shifts among Langdon and other focalizers remain within that person.

search_log: Searched site:danbrown.com and site:penguinrandomhouse.com for The Da Vinci Code excerpts; opened the authorized Dan Brown excerpt, while the Penguin Random House page exposed a sample control but not usable prose.

Searched "The Da Vinci Code" with "point of view," "third person," "narrator," and scholarly terms; opened PALA and Advances in Literary Study analyses that explicitly describe third-person, nonparticipating narration.

Searched for epistolary, frame-narrative, multiple-narrator, and alternating first-/third-person structures; results described changing focal characters within third person and produced no credible evidence of alternating grammatical person.
Searched exact text from q01031, q01033, q01037, and q01041; q01031 remained unattributed, while opened context for q01037 restored the Teabing speech tag.
The Cambridge Companion excerpt located for q01037 timed out when opened, so it was not relied upon; an accessible opened source independently supplied the same dialogue attribution.
person_note: The diagnostic Goodreads passage q01038 agrees with an authorized multi-chapter excerpt and two scholarly structural analyses: the base narrator is a nonparticipating third-person narrator who moves among characters and renders their consciousness. Changes of focalizer do not constitute changes of narrative person. Dialogue, generic maxims, and character thoughts—including locally first-person direct thoughts—are embedded material rather than autonomous first-person sections. The only residual uncertainty is the local attribution of q01031, which is too isolated to affect the well-supported whole-book classification.
